data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A panel of trained non-experts using an explicit checklist is more reliable than a single expert relying on intuition because it transforms a 'synthesis' problem into a 'verification' problem, effectively neutralizing the expert's single-point-of-failure bias.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The task requires the synthesis of non-linear variables not captureable in a linear checklist.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The 'training' of non-experts introduces a shared systemic bias (correlated error) that mirrors the expert's blind spot.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist is poorly designed, omitting the critical variable that the expert's intuition would have caught.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The checklist decomposes a complex judgment into a series of binary, low-cognitive-load verifications. While an expert's intuition (System 1) performs a holistic leap that can be derailed by a single cognitive blind spot or 'heuristic trap', the panel's distributed System 2 process ensures that every required condition is checked. The reliability gain emerges from the statistical improbability of the entire panel missing a checklist item that is explicitly listed, whereas the expert may intuitively 'skip' a step they subconsciously deem irrelevant.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
